body.input: Which AI companies opened an office in Norway in 2026?

response.content:
Based on available information, there is no comprehensive list of AI companies that specifically opened a new office in Norway during 2026. However, several notable AI-related developments in Norway in 2026 include:

- **TEK Norway** opened a dedicated office for promoting the use of artificial intelligence, launching its first programme called "AI to the Thousand" — a two-week initiative to guide companies from exploring AI opportunities to drawing up action plans.

- **Cerebras** has new data centre sites in Norway (and Finland) as part of its capacity expansion, with OpenAI as a major compute customer. Relatedly, **Nscale** (in partnership with Aker, NVIDIA, and Microsoft) has been developing the **Stargate Norway** facility in Narvik. OpenAI withdrew from the Stargate Norway partnership in April 2026, after which **Microsoft** expanded its agreement with Nscale to take the extra compute capacity at that site.

- Norway has also been active in international AI governance: on 9 November 2026, Norway was among six countries (alongside Canada, France, Bahrain, Finland, and the Netherlands) that signed the **Paris Call for AI Safety and Security**, together with companies including Anthropic, Microsoft, OpenAI, Mistral AI, and others.

- On 12 November 2026, the **UK and Norway** signed a **Joint Statement of Intent on Artificial Intelligence**, covering cooperation on compute, defence, AI security, and international governance.

These developments reflect Norway's growing role as an AI infrastructure and policy hub, but specific announcements of AI companies opening traditional offices (as opposed to data centres or partnerships) in Norway in 2026 are limited to the TEK Norway example found above.

explainability.content: The TEK Norway announcement describes that the Norwegian ICT organisation opened a dedicated office to promote AI, confirming an AI‑related office opening in Norway in 2026.
Cerebras reported that its capacity expansion includes new data‑centre sites in Norway, indicating the establishment of AI‑related facilities there in 2026.

The April 2026 filing notes that OpenAI withdrew from the Stargate Norway partnership and Microsoft subsequently expanded its agreement to take the extra compute capacity, showing Microsoft’s involvement in Norwegian AI infrastructure but not a new traditional office.

The Paris Call for AI Safety and Security signed on 9 Nov 2026 lists several AI companies as signatories, but the source material only mentions their participation, not the opening of offices in Norway.
The UK‑Norway Joint Statement of Intent on AI signed on 12 Nov 2026 outlines cooperation on compute and AI security, without indicating any new office openings by AI companies in Norway.

> “That progress energizes us to do even more as we push the limits of innovation and expect to triple revenue in 2027,” Feldman said in the results statement.

For the fourth quarter, Cerebras forecast core revenue of $310m to $330m. Analysts had expected $271m. Tripling revenue in 2027 would mean about $2.85bn, CNBC calculated. That is slightly below the $2.92bn analysts had forecast.

## OpenAI and the capacity problem

Much of the growth rests on OpenAI. Its compute deal underpins Cerebras’ $26.1bn in remaining performance obligations, the contracted revenue it has not yet booked, Reuters reported.

Feldman told analysts that OpenAI’s business with Cerebras grew from the second quarter. But Cerebras did not have the capacity for a broad rollout of OpenAI’s Ultrafast tier, he said. [...] Capacity is where the money is going. Cerebras has 700 megawatts of data centre capacity contracted for delivery by the end of 2027. That includes new sites in Norway and Finland. In the first nine months it used $388.9m in its operations and spent $1.05bn on property and equipment. It ended September with $7.8bn in cash and short-term investments.

Feldman told CNBC the company is weighing its financing options to keep up with demand. On the call, he said data centre availability limits the whole industry. US policy changes could make building harder, he added.

> “As we look to the months ahead, we see two certainties: rapid change and compute shortages,” Feldman told analysts, according to Reuters.

## Chasing Nvidia [...] Cerebras shares rose about 17% in after-hours trading on Thursday. The AI chipmaker posted third-quarter results that beat analysts’ estimates, lifted its outlook for the year and added a new cloud customer.

The company now expects core revenue of $940m to $960m this year, Reuters reported. In August it had forecast $880m to $890m. Core revenue is Cerebras’ adjusted measure. It strips out stock-based pay and some data centre costs. It also adds back the value of share warrants given to customers.

The results statement named the new customer only as “a top three hyperscaler”, with details due next year. Chief executive Andrew Feldman told CNBC’s Jordan Novet that it is Microsoft, which signed in October. He expects revenue from the deal to start arriving in the first quarter of 2027.

The filing also records how quickly partnerships in the sector can change. Nscale announced Stargate Norway in July 2025 and, on September 16, 2025, Stargate UK, a UK infrastructure initiative in partnership with NVIDIA, Microsoft and OpenAI. "In April 2026, OpenAI withdrew from the Stargate Norway and Stargate UK partnerships, with Microsoft subsequently expanding its agreement with us to take the extra compute capacity at Stargate Norway," the risk factors state. [...] Microsoft's ties to Nscale predate that change. In September 2025, PPC Land reported that Microsoft had partnered with Nscale and Aker for a $6.2 billion facility in Narvik, Norway, and with Nscale on a UK supercomputer with more than 23,000 NVIDIA GPUs. OpenAI's retreat from the two Stargate projects came after its chief executive, Sam Altman, had deflected questions in November 2025 about $1.4 trillion in compute commitments over four to five years.

# Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft join 6 nations in AI safety pledge

A person uses a laptop as digital warning symbols, artificial intelligence (AI) icons and data security alerts appear in an illustrative image. (Adobe Stock Photo)
Photo
BigPhoto
Newsletters
Share
newsletters

Countries including Canada, France and Norway, along with technology companies such as Anthropic, Microsoft and OpenAI, have signed a joint declaration on Nov. 9 aimed at ensuring artificial intelligence (AI) safety and security. [...] Titled the “Paris Call for AI Safety and Security,” the declaration was signed by the heads of state and government of Bahrain, Canada, Finland, France, Norway and the Netherlands, along with the chief executives of Anthropic, Black Forest Labs, Cohere, Domyn, Hugging Face, Microsoft, Mistral AI, OpenAI, Sakana AI and Synthesia, according to a statement from the Canadian Prime Minister’s Office.

The statement noted that civil society organizations LawZero, SaferAI, AI Safety Connect and Ifri are also among the signatories, adding that the declaration remains open to new signatories and will continue to be updated. [...] The declaration said the signatories committed to establishing a structured cooperation framework based on three main strategic commitments to put this shared vision into practice.

In this context, they pledged to create a common framework for the evaluation and risk management of advanced AI models, to ensure all actors in the AI ecosystem adhere to the principles of responsibility and accountability, and to develop information sharing and early warning systems.

## What happened

On 9 November 2026, Canada, France, Bahrain, Finland, Norway and the Netherlands signed a joint declaration on a “Paris Call for AI safety and security”, alongside ten AI companies and several civil-society organisations. The Prime Minister’s Office of Canada published the text the same day, and the declaration is non-binding. According to The Next Web, it was agreed at a meeting hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron on the opening day of the Paris Peace Forum.

The statement says it remains open to further endorsements and is being updated, so the list of signatories may change.

## Key details

### Who signed [...] ## Key details

### Who signed

 Governments: Bahrain, Canada, Finland, France, Norway, the Netherlands.
 Companies: Anthropic, Black Forest Labs, Cohere, Domyn, Hugging Face, Microsoft, Mistral AI, OpenAI, Sakana AI, Synthesia.
 Civil society: LawZero (Yoshua Bengio), SaferAI, AI Safety Connect and Ifri are listed in the Canadian text. The Next Web also reports that the French AI safety group CeSIA signed.

The United States is not a signatory, according to The Next Web, and neither are Google, Meta or China.
